- If sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) and prices are trending up, model often fails to adjust downward; apply downward bias correction early in the forecast horizon.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overshoots and fails to correct; cap forecast at 1–2 days after peak or introduce decay factor.
- When sentiment shifts from bullish to bearish (or vice versa), model lags in adjusting mean; apply a 1–3 day lag correction to align with sentiment reversal.
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly while sentiment is strongly bullish, consider mean reversion bias — reduce forecast slope to reflect volatility decay.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome shows early sharp decline after initial rise, model often overestimates early gains; apply downward correction after 5–7 days.
- If sentiment history shows high volatility (alternating 0.33/1.00), model tends to smooth too much — increase forecast variance or allow for sharper transitions.
